ESSENTIALS: Hydration
Dehydration causes fatigue and poor decisions before you even feel thirsty.
Navigation
A map, compass, or downloaded offline maps still work when your phone has no signal or battery.
Insulation
Cascade weather can shift fast — an extra layer keeps a cold snap from becoming hypothermia.
Illumination
A dedicated headlamp means fading daylight doesn’t force you to burn your phone battery.
Combustion
A reliable way to start a fire or heat water matters if you end up out longer than planned.
Communication
A charged phone and a backup way to reach help matter more than almost anything else you carry.
Repair kit
Basic tools and tape fix the small gear failures that turn into big delays.
Sun protection
Sunburn and glare add up fast at elevation and on snow.
Shelter
An emergency bivy or space blanket can get you through a night you didn’t plan for.
First aid
Basic supplies let you manage a minor injury before it becomes a reason to call for help.

A trusted person knows my plan

I understand that little or no cellular service is normal in the backcountry

blocks.text: Across every kind of trouble, these are the moments KCSAR and King County 911 say it’s time to call.

items: You’re genuinely lost, unsafe, or don’t know how to get back safely.
Someone can’t walk, can’t safely self-rescue, or has a serious medical problem.
Your party can’t make reasonable progress toward the trailhead.
A party member is missing and can’t quickly be located or contacted — especially a child, an at-risk adult, or someone injured or under-equipped.
Someone you expected home is overdue and you can’t reach them.

blocks.title: Don’t wait
blocks.text: Don’t wait for darkness or worsening weather to make the call. Calling early is the single biggest thing that changes outcomes.
Call vs. text

Call if you can, text if you can’t. A text should give your location and the type of help you need first, stay short, and skip photos or emoji. Stay available to answer follow-up questions either way.

blocks.title: SAR is free
blocks.text: Search and rescue in Washington is 100% volunteer-driven and provided free of charge. Fear of cost must never prevent or delay calling 911.
The ten systems in the TrailSafe preparation checklist.

items: Hydration. Dehydration causes fatigue and poor decisions before you even feel thirsty.
Navigation. A map, compass, or downloaded offline maps still work when your phone has no signal or battery.
Insulation. Cascade weather can shift fast — an extra layer keeps a cold snap from becoming hypothermia.
Illumination. A dedicated headlamp means fading daylight doesn’t force you to burn your phone battery.
Combustion. A reliable way to start a fire or heat water matters if you end up out longer than planned.
Communication. A charged phone and a backup way to reach help matter more than almost anything else you carry.
Repair kit. Basic tools and tape fix the small gear failures that turn into big delays.
Sun protection. Sunburn and glare add up fast at elevation and on snow.
Shelter. An emergency bivy or space blanket can get you through a night you didn’t plan for.
First aid. Basic supplies let you manage a minor injury before it becomes a reason to call for help.

phone-smart.title: Phone Smart
phone-smart.subtitle: Getting the most from what you carry

blocks.text: A phone is valuable, but it is not enough preparation by itself.

items: Phone fully charged before I leave
Portable battery pack carried
Dedicated headlamp or flashlight carried — not just my phone
Offline maps downloaded in my normal navigation app
A trusted person knows my plan
I know how my satellite messenger or PLB works, if I’m carrying one
My phone’s emergency features (Medical ID, Emergency SOS) are set up
I understand that little or no cellular service is normal in the backcountry

blocks.text: Being found faster often comes down to a few simple, deliberate signals.
Sound and light

items: Use repeated whistle blasts or a light to attract attention. Never start a signal fire where it could create a wildfire or another hazard.
A whistle carries much farther than your voice and costs no energy.
A signal mirror — or any reflective surface — can be seen for miles in good light.
Stomp shapes into snow, lay them out in bright clothing or gear, or build them from rocks or branches.
Make them as large and high-contrast against the ground as you can — bigger is more visible from the air than neat.

blocks.text: If you see or hear a search aircraft

items: Move to open ground if you can do so safely.
Signal in a controlled way — wave both arms overhead, use a mirror, show bright colors.
Never approach an aircraft. Wait for a crew member to approach you or direct you.

blocks.text: A working phone sharing your exact coordinates is usually faster and more precise than any visual signal — use Emergency → Your Location first if you can.

unexpected-overnight.title: Unexpected Overnight
unexpected-overnight.subtitle: Turning a day trip into a safe night out

blocks.text: Being stuck out overnight isn’t a failure — it’s a normal outcome of a trip that ran long, and it’s manageable if you stop and prepare deliberately.

items: Decide early. The moment it’s clear you won’t make it out before dark, stop pushing and start preparing while you still have light.
Pick a site with some wind and water protection, away from cliff edges, loose rock, or dead standing trees.
Get warm and dry before you’re cold, not after — put on every layer you have.
Build or use whatever shelter you’re carrying: an emergency bivy, a space blanket, or a natural windbreak.
Eat and drink what you have — your body needs fuel to stay warm.
Stay together and stay put once you’re settled, unless staying is unsafe.

blocks.text: If you have any signal at all, a short “we’re safe, staying the night, moving at first light” message can prevent a search that didn’t need to happen.
In the morning
Reassess before moving. Daylight often makes a route obvious that felt hopeless in the dark.

blocks.title: If you cannot safely self-rescue
blocks.text: Call 911 early. An overnight message does not cancel an active rescue. Follow dispatcher instructions and stay where rescuers expect you.

cold-hypothermia.title: Cold & Hypothermia
cold-hypothermia.subtitle: The Cascade Concrete hazard, the Umbles, and field rescue

blocks.title: The Deadly PNW Myth: 'It’s Not Even Freezing'
blocks.text: In the Pacific Northwest Cascades and Olympics, the vast majority of Search & Rescue hypothermia emergencies occur in wet, rainy conditions between 35°F and 50°F — NOT in sub-zero winter blizzards. Above-freezing temperatures trick hikers into underestimating exposure, but wet cold strips body heat 25x faster than dry air.
The Science: Why Wet Cold Kills in Under an Hour

items: 1. Water conducts heat 25x faster than air: Saturated clothing (cotton denim, soaked fleece, or wet synthetics) turns your layers into an aggressive thermal siphon. Water conducts heat away from your core 25 times faster than still air.

2. Wind convection strips your thermal blanket: Wind continuously strips the microscopic boundary layer of warm air trapped near the skin. In wet clothes, a 15–25 mph wind causes catastrophic convective cooling.
3. The 45-Minute Drop: Once hiking stops (due to injury, exhaustion, or taking a rest break), core body temperature can plunge into moderate hypothermia in under 45 to 60 minutes.

blocks.text: Recognize it early

Early Warning: The 'Umbles' Checklist. As the brain cools, cerebral coordination deteriorates before the victim realizes they are in danger. Watch your hiking partners closely for the classic 'Umbles':

items: Stumbles (Gross Motor / Ataxia): Tripping on trail roots, clumsy footing, stumbling, lagging behind the group.
Mumbles (Speech & Cognition / Dysarthria): Slurred speech, slow answers to simple questions, confusion, repeating themselves.
Fumbles (Fine Motor): Inability to zip a jacket, tie boot laces, operate headlamp switches, or open snack packages.
Grumbles (Behavior & Attitude): Uncharacteristic apathy, irritability, irrational stubbornness, refusing to put on rain gear or stop.

blocks.title: Critical Red Flag: Shivering Has Stopped
blocks.text: Violent shivering is the body fighting for survival. If a cold, wet hiker STOPS shivering while still cold and exposed, their core body temperature has fallen below 90°F (32°C). This indicates metabolic exhaustion and life-threatening severe hypothermia. Immediate SAR evacuation is required.
SAR Field Protocol: The Hypo Burrito Wrap

items: Stop & shelter immediately: Escape wind and precipitation behind trees, boulders, or inside a tent, tarp, or bothy bag. Continuing to walk in wet wind accelerates heat loss.
Insulate from the cold ground: Place sleeping pads, empty backpacks, or dense evergreen boughs beneath the person. Ground conduction drains heat 3x faster than still air.

Vapor barrier / Hypo burrito wrap: If dry clothes are available, strip wet layers. If NO dry clothes exist, keep wet layers on but wrap the subject inside a waterproof vapor barrier (trash bags, space blanket, bivy) inside a dry sleeping bag to trap humidity and stop evaporative heat loss.

Warm sweet calories (alert only): Give warm, highly sugary fluids (tea with sugar, cocoa, hot cider) ONLY if the subject is fully conscious and swallowing easily. Never force fluids into someone who is drowsy or confused.

Handle gently and keep horizontal: Never force a confused or non-shivering hypothermic subject to exercise. Rough jostling can push cold, acidotic blood from the limbs into the heart, triggering fatal ventricular fibrillation.
Call 911 / Activate SOS: Severe hypothermia cannot be safely re-warmed with a campfire on the trail; it requires SAR evacuation and hospital core rewarming.

blocks.text: Prevention principle: 'Cotton kills.' Never wear cotton socks, jeans, or t-shirts in the backcountry. Put on your waterproof shell BEFORE your clothes become damp, and add an insulating layer as soon as you stop hiking.

sources: Mountaineering: The Freedom of the Hills (Hypothermia & Cold Weather Safety)

heat.title: Heat
heat.subtitle: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke on trail

blocks.text: Heat problems can become serious quickly, especially on exposed trail. Stop exertion and get out of the heat.
Heat exhaustion

items: Heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, nausea, and weakness can be warning signs.
Move to shade, loosen excess clothing, and cool the skin with water and wet cloths.
Sip water only if fully alert and able to swallow. Seek medical help if vomiting, worsening, or symptoms persist.

blocks.title: Possible heat stroke — call 911
blocks.text: Confusion, slurred speech, collapse, or a very high body temperature is an emergency. The person may still be sweating. Call 911 and begin cooling immediately; follow dispatcher instructions. Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious.

winter-safety.title: Winter Travel
winter-safety.subtitle: Snow travel, avalanche awareness, and short days

blocks.text: Winter adds three compounding risks: cold, short daylight, and terrain that can behave very differently under snow.
Before you go

items: Check the avalanche forecast for your specific zone at nwac.us if you’ll be in or under steep, snow-loaded terrain.
Know your route’s daylight window — winter days can end by mid-afternoon.
Carry traction and know how to use it before you need it.

blocks.title: Avalanche terrain needs specific training
blocks.text: Companion rescue and terrain assessment aren’t taught in this app. Without that training, stay out of steep, open avalanche terrain and the runout below it.
On the trail

items: Trail markers, cairns, and the trail itself can disappear under snow — navigation skills matter more, not less.
Cold drains phone batteries fast; keep it warm against your body.
Wet snow soaks insulation quickly; waterproof outer layers matter.

blocks.text: See also: Cold & Hypothermia, and Satellite Messengers & PLBs for winter communications.

satellite-plb.title: Satellite Messengers & PLBs
satellite-plb.subtitle: Devices that work with no cell service

blocks.text: These devices send for help from places your phone can’t — but they work differently, and it’s worth knowing which is which before you’re relying on one.
Satellite messengers

items: Send two-way text messages and an SOS via satellite.
Usually require a paid subscription plan.
Battery and satellite view matter — test yours before you rely on it.

blocks.text: Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs)

items: Send a one-way distress signal with your GPS location to a national search-and-rescue system.
No subscription required — but no two-way messaging either.
Must be registered (in the US, with NOAA) to your name and emergency contacts.

blocks.text: Either device needs a clear sky view to work — dense tree cover, canyons, and being inside a tent can all weaken the signal. Learn your device’s SOS trigger before you need it.
Carrying a satellite device doesn’t replace a trip plan or the Ten Essentials — it’s one more layer, not a substitute for the others.

backcountry-radio.title: Backcountry Radio
backcountry-radio.subtitle: What FRS, GMRS, and ham radio can and can’t do

blocks.text: A handheld radio can help keep your own party in contact — but it isn’t a reliable way to call for rescue.
What FRS / GMRS radios do well

items: Keep a spread-out party in contact over short, line-of-sight distances.
Work with no cell service and, for FRS, no license or subscription.
GMRS offers more power and repeater access, and requires an FCC license.

blocks.text: What they don’t do

items: Generally won’t reach 911 or a specific rescue team directly.
Range drops sharply in canyons, dense forest, and around ridgelines.
Battery life is limited, like any other electronic device.

blocks.text: Ham radio

For licensed operators, ham radio and repeaters can sometimes extend range — but this requires training and licensing this app doesn’t provide. Do not assume any channel or repeater is monitored by SAR.
Treat radio as a way to stay together as a party, not your primary way to summon rescue — a phone, satellite messenger, or PLB does that job better.

children-family.title: Hiking with Kids
children-family.subtitle: Preventing separation and preparing kids to wait

blocks.text: Most of preventing a lost child comes down to a few minutes of preparation before you start walking.
Before you go

items: Dress kids in bright, easy-to-spot colors.
Give each child a whistle and teach them: three blasts means “I need help.”
Take a phone photo of what each child is wearing that morning.
Agree on a simple rule before you start: if separated, stop and stay put.

blocks.text: Teaching kids to wait to be found

A well-known wilderness-safety lesson for children is simple: if you’re lost, stay in one place, make yourself big and visible, and make noise — rather than wandering to try to find the trail yourself. A child who stays put is dramatically easier to find than one who keeps moving.
If a child goes missing
Follow the Party Separation guide, and tell 911 the child’s age, clothing, and whether they’ve been taught to stay put — it changes how a search is run.

wildlife.title: Wildlife Encounters
wildlife.subtitle: Bears, cougars, and staying safe around wildlife

blocks.text: Most wildlife encounters end with the animal leaving — your job is mostly to avoid surprising it, and to respond calmly if you don’t.
General principles

items: Make noise on trail, especially near streams, thick brush, or blind corners, so animals have time to move off.
Keep food secured and away from your sleeping area overnight.
Keep dogs leashed — an off-leash dog can provoke an encounter, then run back to you with an animal behind it.

blocks.text: Black bears

items: Stay calm, back away slowly, don’t run. Make yourself look bigger and speak in a firm, calm voice.

blocks.text: Cougars

items: Do not run. Maintain eye contact, make yourself look big, and pick up small children. Back away slowly; fight back if attacked.

blocks.text: Snakes

items: Give any snake a wide path and let it move away on its own. Watch where you place hands and feet on rocky terrain.

blocks.text: Mountain goats

items: Stay at least 50 yards away. Goats aggressively seek salt from human sweat — never let them lick gear or clothing.
Urinate on rocks or gravel well away from trails, not on trailside vegetation, which attracts goats to the path.
They can be dangerously aggressive. Give them space and do not approach for photos.

blocks.text: Ticks

items: Wear light-colored clothing so ticks are easier to spot. Tuck pants into socks in brushy areas.
Use permethrin on clothing and DEET or picaridin on exposed skin.
Perform a full-body tick check after every hike. Remove attached ticks with fine-tipped tweezers, pulling straight out.

blocks.text: For current, location-specific wildlife guidance, see Washington Dept. of Fish & Wildlife under Resources.

lessons-learned.title: Lessons from Real Rescues
lessons-learned.subtitle: Patterns KCESAR volunteers see again and again

blocks.text: These are common patterns, told as composites rather than specific case files — the small decisions that come up again and again.
The trail that used to be obvious
Fresh snow, fallen leaves, or fog erased a route the hiker had done many times before, and familiarity stood in for navigation. Lesson: carry and use a map even on trails you know well.
Just a little further
A short planned hike stretched to an hour, then two, chasing a viewpoint that always looked just ahead. Lesson: set a turnaround time before you leave, and honor it even when the summit feels close.
Nobody knew the route

A solo hiker said “going for a hike” with no route, no time, and no trailhead written down. When they didn’t return, searchers had almost nothing to go on. Lesson: a trip plan only helps if someone actually has it.
The phone that couldn’t reach anyone

A hiker could see a signal indicator but could not complete a call. Lesson: try texting if a call cannot connect. Do not roam or enter hazardous terrain for reception. If in contact with 911, stay where responders expect you unless staying is immediately unsafe.
Decide at home, not on the mountain

Physical fatigue reduces cognitive function, time pressure creates poor choices, and emotional investment in your goal can override safety concerns. Make critical decisions — turnaround time, weather go/no-go, bailout routes — at home when your judgment is clear. Plan for 50% longer than your most optimistic estimate.
Following strangers off-route

Two hikers missed a junction, met another group who casually suggested a different route, followed them, lost the other party, and ended up off-trail. A well-meaning family member then tried to remotely guide them by phone and got them even further lost. Lesson: stick to your researched plan, don't follow strangers' route suggestions, and if you're lost, call 911 rather than having someone at home try to guide you.
The group that scattered

A group of friends let faster hikers pull ahead on a descent. One person missed a junction and kept going. Hours later, nobody could account for everyone. Lesson: hike at the pace of the slowest member, assign a sweep at the rear, and regroup at every trail junction. Never let anyone separate from the group.
Water crossings are one of the most dangerous moments on a backcountry trip. Snowmelt-fed streams can change from ankle-deep in the morning to thigh-deep by afternoon.

items: Unbuckle your hip belt and chest strap before crossing so you can jettison your pack if you're swept off your feet.
Cross at wide, braided, shallow sections — never at narrow gorges where the water runs deep and fast.
Face upstream, lean slightly forward into the current, and shuffle your feet rather than lifting them high.
Use trekking poles for a third point of contact.
Never cross water above thigh depth, or fast-moving water above knee depth.
Keep your footwear on — bare feet lead to foot entrapment between rocks and puncture injuries.
Time of day matters: snowmelt crossings are lowest in early morning and highest in late afternoon.

blocks.title: When in doubt
blocks.text: If the crossing looks dangerous, turn around. No destination is worth drowning.

clothing-layering.title: Clothing & Layering
clothing-layering.subtitle: Why cotton kills and what to wear instead

blocks.text: Wet clothing in cool, windy weather is a direct path to hypothermia. What you wear matters as much as what you carry.
The layering system

items: Base layer: synthetic or merino wool to wick sweat away from your skin.
Mid layer: insulating fleece, wool, or synthetic puff jacket.
Outer shell: waterproof, windproof, breathable jacket with taped seams. In the Pacific Northwest, always have a rain layer.

blocks.title: Cotton kills
blocks.text: Cotton retains moisture, loses all insulation when wet, and dramatically accelerates hypothermia. No cotton socks, jeans, or t-shirts on the trail.
Winter additions

items: Pack dry socks, insulated gloves, a warm hat, and a dry base layer in your pack — even if you're already wearing layers.
Keep your phone in an inner pocket against body heat. Cold temperatures rapidly drain lithium-ion batteries.

blocks.title: STOP
blocks.text: Stop moving. Stay calm. You will think more clearly standing still than while wandering.

items: Stop moving and stay calm.
Think: when did you last know exactly where you were?
Observe your surroundings, resources, weather, daylight, and hazards.
Plan — don't make the situation worse.

blocks.title: If you are genuinely lost, unsafe, or don't know how to get back safely
blocks.text: Call 911. Do not wait for darkness or worsening weather.
If you're already in contact with 911 or SAR
Stay where you are unless a dispatcher or rescuer tells you to move, or you must move a short distance to reach immediate safety.
Additional actions

items: Get out of any immediate hazard.

Don't assume a creek or drainage leads safely downhill to a road or town. In Cascade terrain, drainages can lead into waterfalls, cliffs, canyons, and dense brush. If you're genuinely lost, stop and call rather than following this common myth.
Keep your party together.
Put on insulation before you get cold, not after.
Prepare shelter if conditions warrant it.
Make yourself visible.
Preserve your phone battery.
Answer calls or texts from unknown numbers while a rescue is active.
Follow dispatcher or rescuer instructions over anything in this app.
Make the scene safe so there aren't more victims.
Address immediate life threats using the first-aid skills you actually have.
If the person can't safely self-rescue, has a serious injury or illness, or you're unsure — call 911 early.
Give an exact location and describe the patient's condition.
Protect the person from cold, wet ground, wind, rain, or heat.
Stay available to 911 and follow their instructions.

blocks.text: Inability to walk, inability to safely self-rescue, a serious medical problem, or being unable to make reasonable progress toward the trailhead are all good reasons to call 911.
This app doesn't try to diagnose or treat medical conditions. For anything beyond basic first aid, defer to your training and to 911.
Exhaustion, terrain beyond your ability, gear failure, darkness, or impassable snow or water can all leave you unable to safely continue.

items: Stop before exhaustion or darkness turns this into an injury.
Move only as much as necessary to reach a safe location.
Evaluate daylight, weather, clothing, shelter, food, water, and communications.
If you can't safely self-rescue, or you're unsure — call 911.
Prepare to stay warm, stay dry, and wait.

blocks.title: Call before it becomes catastrophic
blocks.text: It's normal — and expected — to call for help before a manageable problem turns into an emergency.
If separation just occurred

items: Stop the rest of the group from scattering.
Identify the last place and time everyone was together.
Try normal contact methods.
Don't send multiple uncoordinated people off searching in different directions.

blocks.text: Call 911 when

items: The missing person can't quickly be located or contacted.
They're a child, an at-risk adult, injured, or inadequately equipped.
Darkness, weather, or terrain raise the urgency.

blocks.text: Have this ready for 911

items: Name and age
Clothing and pack description
Medical considerations
Phone or device number
Last known point and intended route
Experience level and footwear, if useful

blocks.text: Is the person overdue and you can't reach them?

items: Try the phone or contact method on their trip plan.
Review the intended return time and the "if you have not heard from me by" time.
Gather their complete trip plan.
If they remain overdue and can't be contacted — call 911.

Tell 911 they're overdue from an outdoor trip and provide names, party size, planned route, trailhead, timing, vehicle, clothing, communications devices, and any medical or experience information you know.

blocks.text: An overdue outdoor traveler who can't be contacted is a legitimate reason to call 911 — you don't need to wait longer to be sure.

items: If contacting 911, give your location and the type of help needed first.
Stay available to answer follow-up questions.
Follow dispatcher or responder instructions over anything in this app.
Move only as needed for immediate safety.

blocks.text: Once you've called for help, this is what actually helps.

items: Follow the 911 call taker's or rescuer's instructions over anything in this app.
Stay where rescuers expect you unless staying is immediately unsafe.
Keep your party together.
Prevent further injury.
Get warm and dry early — don't wait until you feel cold.
Make yourself visible.
Keep communication devices accessible.

blocks.text: Preserve your battery

items: Turn on Low Power Mode — it preserves calls and messages while reducing other power use.
Reduce screen brightness and let the screen sleep when you're not using it.
Stop optional high-power activities like recording video.
Don't force-close apps as a generic battery-saving step.
Don't blindly disable cellular, Wi-Fi, or Bluetooth — those may be needed for a 911 callback, messaging, or a paired satellite device. Only turn off what you know is unnecessary.

blocks.text: Help rescuers find you

items: Don't repeatedly call 911 for status updates unless instructed or the situation changes.
Be ready to describe nearby landmarks, sounds, terrain, trail signs, water, roads, or other features.
If you hear or see searchers or aircraft, signal in a controlled, obvious way.
Never approach an aircraft unless a crew member directs you to.

blocks.text: If a helicopter arrives

items: Secure all loose gear — sleeping pads, pack covers, and jackets become dangerous projectiles in rotor wash.
Stay low and crouched when the helicopter is nearby.
Never walk toward the tail rotor — it is invisible when spinning and instantly lethal.
Wait for crew to approach you and give explicit instructions before moving.
